sources.news_title: Donald Trump's Former White House Aide Avoids Indictment in New Legal Twist
sources.text:
Donald Trump‘s former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson reportedly avoids indictment over her testimony to a congressional panel. The decision came amid the Justice Department’s investigation into whether Hutchinson gave false testimony.
Grand jury rejects indictment of former Trump aide Cassidy Hutchinson over January 6 testimony
The grand jury “no bill” decision means it declined to approve the proposed indictment. The investigation focused on Hutchinson’s testimony to a congressional panel about the January 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol by Trump’s supporters.
According to Reuters, a source confirmed the jury met on Tuesday and was considering the evidence in the probe, but did not know the decision. A former prosecutor separately told US Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui in court that the federal jury rejected an indictment but did not share the proposed defendant or charges.
The Justice Department has been investigating Cassidy Hutchinson over whether she gave false testimony for the probe. However, she maintained her stance on her testimony.
Weeks after Trump falsely claimed he had won the 2020 elections, his supporters marched to the U.S. Capitol on January 6, 2021, in an attempt to stop congressional certification of elections. However, the attack failed to stop Congress, and many people were subsequently charged with crimes. Trump pardoned almost everyone who faced charges on his first day of his second presidency term in 2025.
Hutchinson’s case was handled by the Civil Rights Division headed by Trump appointee Harmeet Dhillon. She made several claims regarding Trump’s behavior in the days up to January 6, 2021. Hutchinson testified that Trump urged the removal of metal detectors. She quoted Trump’s words at the time of the incidents, saying, “not here to hurt me” and “I don’t f—ing care that they have weapons.” (via NBC News)
Her testimony also included accounts of Trump’s actions on January 6, 2021, his response to supporters, and Trump’s alleged attempt to reach Capitol. The grand jury reportedly heard the evidence in early October, but did not secure an indictment despite investigation into her testimony.

Federal Grand Jury Refuses to Indict Cassidy Hutchinson After Disputed Testimony About President Trump
A federal grand jury in Washington, D.C., declined Tuesday to indict former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson, rejecting the Justice Department’s attempt to pursue criminal charges stemming from her controversial testimony about President Trump’s actions on January 6, 2021.
The decision follows an investigation into whether Hutchinson provided false information to Congress when she testified before the House committee investigating the Capitol riot in June 2022.
According to people familiar with the proceedings, federal prosecutors presented evidence seeking an indictment, but grand jurors declined to approve the proposed charges.
The rejection represents a setback for the Justice Department, although it does not establish whether Hutchinson’s testimony was truthful or inaccurate.
Hutchinson, who served as a special assistant to White House Chief of Staff Mark Meadows during Trump’s first administration, became a prominent witness in the congressional investigation after delivering testimony that attracted national attention.
Her most widely discussed allegation involved an account of President Trump supposedly attempting to grab the steering wheel of his presidential vehicle after Secret Service personnel refused to transport him to the Capitol.
Hutchinson acknowledged during her testimony that she had not personally witnessed the alleged confrontation. Instead, she said she learned about it from then-White House Deputy Chief of Staff Tony Ornato.
President Trump strongly denied the allegation, describing Hutchinson as a “total phony” and disputing her account of his behavior.
The controversy intensified in March 2024 when House Republicans released previously undisclosed testimony from the Secret Service agent who drove the presidential vehicle that day.
The driver directly contradicted the allegation that Trump attempted to seize the steering wheel or physically lunge toward the front of the vehicle.
His testimony nevertheless confirmed that Trump had wanted to travel to the Capitol after addressing supporters near the White House.
Those conflicting accounts became central to Republican criticism of Hutchinson and the congressional committee that relied on her testimony.
Republican lawmakers subsequently accused Hutchinson of providing misleading information under oath and referred the matter to federal authorities for potential prosecution.
Hutchinson has maintained that she testified truthfully about what she knew and what others had told her.
The latest investigation was handled by the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, according to reporting from CBS News.
During an unrelated federal court hearing Tuesday, Justice Department attorney Neville Hedley informed U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui that a grand jury had declined to approve a proposed indictment.
Hedley did not publicly identify the individual involved, but multiple people familiar with the proceedings confirmed that the rejected indictment concerned Hutchinson.
The precise allegations and evidence presented to grand jurors have not been publicly disclosed in full.
ABC News reported that prosecutors had sought charges involving allegedly false statements to Congress.
The Justice Department had not issued a detailed public explanation of the grand jury’s decision as of Tuesday evening.
Grand juries determine whether prosecutors have established probable cause to bring criminal charges. They do not decide whether a defendant is guilty.
An indictment ordinarily requires agreement from at least 12 members of a federal grand jury, which can consist of between 16 and 23 people.
When a grand jury declines to indict, prosecutors cannot proceed on the rejected indictment, although they may sometimes pursue additional evidence or present a revised case.
The decision therefore leaves Hutchinson without criminal charges arising from this particular presentation of evidence.
The case has renewed attention on the congressional investigation into January 6 and the disputed accounts presented during its public hearings.
Hutchinson testified at a nationally televised hearing arranged with approximately one day’s notice, describing conversations and events she said occurred inside the White House before and during the Capitol riot.
In addition to the presidential vehicle allegation, she testified that Trump wanted security screening equipment removed near his rally because some attendees carrying weapons were not there to harm him.
She also described conversations involving Meadows and other senior officials as the situation at the Capitol deteriorated.
Her testimony became an important part of the committee’s public presentation of events surrounding the certification of the 2020 presidential election.
However, the secondhand nature of her account about the presidential vehicle drew particular scrutiny.
House Republicans later argued that the committee had placed substantial emphasis on an allegation contradicted by testimony from a person who was actually present.
The Secret Service driver’s account established a significant factual disagreement about the alleged physical confrontation, although it did not contradict every aspect of Hutchinson’s testimony.
Hutchinson has consistently maintained that she accurately conveyed what she was told.
She has also alleged that individuals associated with Trump’s political circle attempted to influence her cooperation with congressional investigators.
According to her testimony, she was offered potential employment opportunities and financial assistance while participating in the investigation.
She further alleged that an attorney representing her at the time encouraged her to limit what she disclosed to the committee.
Those claims became part of the broader congressional inquiry and were separate from the question of whether her testimony about the presidential vehicle was knowingly false.
Proving a criminal false-statement offense requires more than demonstrating that a witness repeated an account later contradicted by another person.
Prosecutors generally must establish that a materially false statement was made knowingly and willfully.
That distinction is especially important when testimony involves information a witness says was received from someone else.
Even if the underlying account proves inaccurate, criminal liability can depend on what the witness actually knew and intended when testifying.
The grand jury’s refusal to indict does not provide a public explanation of which evidentiary or legal issues influenced its decision.
Hutchinson’s testimony remains part of the historical record of the congressional investigation.
President Trump was impeached by the House in January 2021 on a charge of incitement of insurrection following the Capitol riot, but the Senate subsequently acquitted him.
A separate federal criminal case brought by special counsel Jack Smith concerning Trump’s efforts to challenge the 2020 election was abandoned after his victory in the 2024 presidential election.
The Justice Department cited its longstanding policy against prosecuting a sitting president when ending that case.
Trump has continued disputing the conclusions reached by the January 6 committee and has criticized several witnesses and investigators associated with its work.
The administration’s investigation of Hutchinson developed against that backdrop, with Republican lawmakers seeking accountability for testimony they believed was misleading.
Hutchinson, meanwhile, has continued defending her account and rejecting allegations that she deliberately deceived Congress.
The grand jury decision is also notable because prosecutors ordinarily obtain indictments when they present evidence sufficient to establish probable cause.
A refusal is relatively uncommon, particularly in high-profile federal investigations.
Nevertheless, grand jurors retain independent authority to reject proposed charges when they are not persuaded that the legal standard has been satisfied.
For now, Hutchinson will not face prosecution based on the indictment rejected Tuesday.
The Justice Department has not announced whether it intends to pursue additional investigative steps or make another attempt to secure charges.
The outcome leaves unresolved the longstanding disagreement over Hutchinson’s testimony, particularly her secondhand account of the alleged confrontation inside the presidential vehicle.
While the former White House aide has maintained that she told Congress the truth, President Trump and Republican lawmakers have continued challenging the reliability of her statements.
Tuesday’s decision settles the immediate question of whether the grand jury would authorize the proposed prosecution, but it does not resolve every factual dispute surrounding her testimony.

The former staffer’s testimony focused on Trump’s actions that day

In her account, he sought to allow armed protesters to bypass security screenings at a rally held to protest his 2020 election loss. She also stated that he grabbed the steering wheel of the presidential SUV once the Secret Service refused to drive him to the Capitol.
She further testified that Trump did not act when the crowd at the Capitol began chanting “Hang Mike Pence.” Trump rejected much of her description at the time. On Truth Social he labeled her a “total phony” and “bad news.”

In 2021, the House of Representatives impeached Trump on the grounds that he incited the mob that stormed the Capitol, though the Senate voted to acquit him. Hutchinson grew up in Pennington, New Jersey. Before joining the White House, she worked in the office of legislative affairs and completed internships with Republican members of Congress, among them Representative Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Senator Ted Cruz of Texas.

sources.news_title: Trump’s Bid to Prosecute Jan. 6 Witness Cassidy Hutchinson Fails as Grand Jury Rejects Indictment
sources.text:
Donald Trump’s Justice Department just suffered another legal blow in its effort to prosecute one of the former White House aides whose testimony helped expose the chaos surrounding January 6.
A federal grand jury in Washington, D.C., has refused to indict Cassidy Hutchinson, the former White House aide who delivered explosive testimony about Trump’s actions on the day his supporters stormed the U.S. Capitol. The decision, reported Tuesday by The Washington Post and other major news outlets, leaves prosecutors without the indictment they sought.
The case centered on allegations that Hutchinson lied under oath during her 2022 testimony to the House committee investigating January 6. Trump and his Republican allies have spent years attacking her account and pushing for legal consequences.
But when prosecutors brought the proposed case before a grand jury, they failed to secure an indictment.
In a court appearance Tuesday, Justice Department attorney Neville S. Hedley told U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia M. Faruqui that the grand jury had not agreed to the proposed indictment. Hedley did not name the person involved, but sources familiar with the matter identified Hutchinson as the intended defendant.
For the Trump administration, the outcome is another embarrassing obstacle in a series of politically sensitive prosecutions that have faced resistance from grand juries and the courts.
Hutchinson became a central figure in the January 6 investigation because of her proximity to Trump’s inner circle. She served as an aide to then-White House chief of staff Mark Meadows and testified publicly in June 2022 about what she said she witnessed and learned during the days surrounding the Capitol attack.
Her account portrayed Trump as angry and determined to reach the Capitol as his supporters gathered in Washington to protest his 2020 election loss.
Hutchinson testified that Trump knew some of his supporters were armed and wanted to join the crowd heading toward the Capitol despite security concerns.
One of the most explosive parts of her testimony involved an alleged confrontation inside the presidential SUV, known as “The Beast.” Hutchinson said another White House official told her Trump lunged toward the front of the vehicle and reached for the steering wheel after the Secret Service refused to take him to the Capitol.
That account was disputed. The agent who drove the vehicle later said he did not see Trump lunge toward the front seat and stated that Trump never grabbed the steering wheel. Hutchinson acknowledged during her testimony that she was relaying what another official had told her rather than describing an incident she witnessed firsthand.
She also testified about Trump’s reaction to chants of “Hang Mike Pence” as rioters threatened the vice president. Her account became a major part of the committee’s effort to document Trump’s conduct before and during the attack.
Trump rejected Hutchinson’s testimony and publicly attacked her credibility.
The investigation into Hutchinson followed referrals from Republican Reps. Barry Loudermilk and Jim Jordan, who accused her of providing false testimony to Congress.
Their efforts helped move the matter to the Justice Department, which ultimately sought an indictment. The specific allegations prosecutors intended to bring were not immediately made public in the reporting on the grand jury’s decision.
The case was handled by the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, an unusual choice for an investigation centered on allegedly false statements, according to The Washington Post.
Grand juries generally approve indictments when prosecutors present sufficient evidence to establish probable cause, making a rejection an unusual outcome.
The failed effort comes as the Trump administration pursues other high-profile cases involving figures the president has publicly criticized.
Among them is former FBI Director James Comey, who has faced another attempt by federal prosecutors to bring charges. Federal authorities have also searched the home of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar as part of a separate investigation.
These cases involve different allegations and legal circumstances, but the Hutchinson decision adds to scrutiny of the Justice Department’s pursuit of Trump’s perceived adversaries.
The grand jury’s rejection leaves the administration without the criminal case it sought against a witness whose testimony about Trump has continued to provoke the president’s anger.
After years of Trump and his allies demanding that Hutchinson face consequences, the latest development is a clear defeat for this prosecution effort — and another reminder that political pressure does not guarantee prosecutors will get the outcome they want.

Trump’s Attempt to Punish Cassidy Hutchinson Ends in a Flop
A grand jury failed to indict the former White House aide.
Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty Images
The Trump administration’s attempt to prosecute former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson over her testimony to the House January 6 committee has hit a snag.
A federal grand jury in Washington, D.C., declined to indict Hutchinson, The Washington Postreported Tuesday evening, citing two anonymous sources. Neville S. Hedley, who told U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia M. Faruqui earlier that day that he was acting senior litigation counsel at the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, had warned in court that the jury could not agree on an indictment. Hedley didn’t mention a name, but the Post’s sources said it was Hutchinson.
President Donald Trump and his Republican allies have been seeking charges against Hutchinson for months, accusing her of lying to the investigative committee. In March, Representative Barry Loudermilk referred her to the Department of Justice, and House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan signed off on it.
Hutchinson was one of the star witnesses in the committee’s hearings, claiming that Trump was very agitated on January 6, 2021, and fully aware of the potential for violence. She testified that he wanted to march with his supporters on the Capitol, and was furious when his aides and Secret Service detail said that it wouldn’t be safe.
Trump even tried to grab the steering wheel of the presidential limousine known as The Beast, and when a Secret Service agent took his arm, Trump grabbed the agent’s neck, Hutchinson said. Along with then–White House chief of staff Mark Meadows, she said that Trump wanted his armed supporters to march that day, and overheard a conversation where Trump said that Mike Pence “deserves it,” regarding chants of “hang Mike Pence” heard during the riot.
For now, though, Hutchinson won’t face criminal charges, although MAGA Republicans may try to indict her again. Trump keeps trying to settle old scores in his second term as president. For instance, his Department of Justice just charged former FBI Director James Comey for a third time.
Judge Trashes DOJ Attempt to Add More Charges Over Hunter Biden Laptop
Federal prosecutors failed to get judicial approval before filing a new criminal complaint against two former FBI officials who investigated Hunter Biden.
Hunter Biden
Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty Images
Hunter Biden
A federal judge tore into Department of Justice prosecutors Tuesday for attempting to file a new criminal complaint alleging that two ex-FBI agents had lied to Congress during the investigation into Hunter Biden’s laptop.
At a hearing, Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui refused to rubber-stamp a superseding complaint, which would have added an obstruction charge against former intelligence analyst Nikki Floris, who ran the intelligence division at the Washington field office, and Bradley Benavides, a former deputy assistant director for counterintelligence.
Faruqui told the prosecutors that if they wanted to file a superseding complaint, then a judge would first have to find probable cause that a crime had actually been committed. Instead, the government had transmitted the complaint in the middle of the night and expected the judge to sign it.
Faruqui said that he believed the government had broken precedent by seeking a superseding complaint without first receiving a judge’s signature.
“I’m concerned with your view as to what the law is,” he said. “Why today, on this one case, have you changed the entire history of how you charge cases?”
After Floris and Benavides surrendered on arrest warrants last week, Faruqui had ordered a hearing on Tuesday in order to establish probable cause for the initial complaint. Notably, the DOJ did not obtain a grand jury indictment against the ex-officials.
On Monday night, the government submitted an unsworn affidavit it claimed would support an additional obstruction charge. Faruqui refused to sign the complaint without reviewing it or finding probable cause, and proceeded to hold the hearing on just the first complaint.
Todd Blanche Basically Coached Ghislaine Maxwell in Epstein Interview
House Democrats’ report revealed how much Blanche helped Maxwell during the interview.
Attorney General Todd Blanche
Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
Attorney General Todd Blanche
Attorney General Todd Blanche’s July 2025 interviews with convicted sex trafficker Ghislaine Maxwell were reportedly a calculated effort to steer public blowback from the Epstein files away from Donald Trump.
House Judiciary Committee Democrats released a 50-page report on Monday accusing the Trump administration of a vast cover-up of the president’s involvement in Jeffrey Epstein’s criminal sex schemes. The report cites the experiences of 11 women, FBI records, and documents released through the Epstein Files Transparency Act. But one detail in the sprawling investigation hinted at an explicit attempt by Blanche to keep Maxwell from implicating the president in Epstein’s crimes.
Blanche notably did not ask Maxwell any questions about a certain Jane Doe, despite the fact that she was on the FBI’s radar for alleging that Trump attempted to orally rape her and subsequently punched her in the head when she was 14 years old.
At one point in the interview, Blanche vaguely mentioned testimony that alleged Epstein and Trump were involved with a 14-year-old, asking if Maxwell recalled “any obviously under-18 women coming to give him a massage?”
Maxwell volunteered that she believed Blanche was “talking about Jane.” But Blanche didn’t bite, instead responding simply, “yeah”—evidence that he was aware of the victim’s accusations.
As soon as Maxwell began to address Jane’s claims, Blanche “cut her off and instructed her not to share specifics,” according to the report. At other points, Blanche interrupted Maxwell to redirect her attention away from Jane’s allegations, arguing that he didn’t want to “get into … he said, she said.”
“Absolutely, not. I’m not—I don’t want to go there either,” Maxwell responded, adding, “I’m not going to do that.”
Maxwell tried to independently mention Jane later in the interview but was again shut down by Blanche, who abruptly cut her off to say he didn’t want to “talk about individuals.”
“The whole point of the conversation was not to uncover information but to create a conspiracy of silence and strategically deter Ghislaine Maxwell from sharing information that was not public at the time regarding the relationship between Trump and Epstein,” the report alleges.
Brazil’s Flávio Bolsonaro Flees to U.S. After Election Defeat
Brazil’s far-right presidential candidate wants to claim political asylum in the United States, sources say.
Presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro looks on after the results of Brazil’s general election were reported on October 25.
Ton Molina/Getty Images
Presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro looks on after the results of Brazil’s general election were reported on October 25.
Flávio Bolsonaro has fled to the United States after losing Brazil’s presidential election to incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Brazil on Sunday, according to multiple outlets.
Bolsonaro’s allies reported his escape to CNN Brasil, and Reuters also confirmed he is headed to the United States, citing two sources.
Brazilian outlet O Globo reported that the far-right senator “was convinced he could be arrested.” While both Bolsonaro’s departure point and destination are uncertain, another Brazilian outlet, Metropoles, reported that he was on his way to Florida to seek asylum. Bolsonaro’s father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is currently serving out house arrest in Brazil for attempting his own version of January 6. He also fled to Florida in late 2022 briefly before his arrest.
Bolsonaro, who has still not conceded the election to Lula, had his passport canceled by the Brazilian Supreme Court due to an active money-laundering case against him. He had until 11 a.m. Tuesday to turn his passport in, but of course didn’t show—fueling questions about his whereabouts.
The Trump administration has been quite friendly to Bolsonaro’s family and antagonistic toward Lula’s left-leaning government.
Neither Bolsonaro nor the U.S. State Department have made a public statement.
Supreme Court Strips Judges of Power to Pause Trump Deportations
The Supreme Court is allowing Trump to block immigration judges from postponing some deportation cases.
Children wait outside an immigration court in New York City, on July 31.
Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images
Children wait outside an immigration court in New York City, on July 31.
The Supreme Court ruled Tuesday that immigration judges can’t postpone deportation cases, giving President Trump another tool in his mass deportation agenda.
The court denied an emergency request to reinstate administrative closure, the practice that allows judges to temporarily delay deportation cases, after the Trump administration made an agreement with the state of Texas to end it in June. The request came from three cities—Baltimore; New Haven, Connecticut; and Columbus, Ohio—and from nonprofit legal aid organization Centro Legal de la Raza.
The court’s denial was one sentence long without any explanation, a standard practice for emergency requests, and there were no reported dissents.
The agreement to end administrative closure was made in federal court in Texas on the same day the state sued to challenge the practice. A judge also approved the agreement the same day, which the plaintiffs cited in their lawsuit as proof the White House colluded with Texas to get rid of the rule.
“The need for interim relief is underscored by the collusion that infected this suit from its inception,” the cities and organization wrote.
Administrative closure used to be common, with immigration judges using the tool to clear packed dockets, especially when a person had proceedings that could prevent their deportation such as a visa petition or appeal of a criminal conviction. Conservative politicians in places like Texas argue that the practice allows immigrants without legal status to stay in the country indefinitely.
The Biden administration tried to make the practice permanent in 2024, but after Trump returned to the White House, the Department of Justice announced it would no longer defend administrative closure. Tuesday’s ruling follows Friday’s federal appeals court decision that immigrants aren’t entitled to bond hearings. In less than a week, the Trump administration has successfully eroded immigration law in order to deport more people.

Published 12:05 am Wednesday, October 28, 2026
A federal grand jury in Washington on Tuesday rejected an effort by the Justice Department to indict Cassidy Hutchinson, the former White House aide President Donald Trump targeted after she gave damning testimony to a congressional committee investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, according to people briefed on the matter.

Some Justice Department prosecutors had been deeply skeptical that there was a case to be made against Hutchinson, concluding that it would be difficult to win a conviction against her.
But in an unusual arrangement, the investigation was directed to the department’s civil rights division, which normally focuses on issues like police violence and election integrity. The civil rights division is led by Harmeet Dhillon, a Trump loyalist who has effectively reoriented the unit to align with Trump’s agenda, including by extracting agreements from elite universities that were favorable to the administration.
It was once rare for grand jurors to rebuff prosecutors and turn down a request for an indictment, given that the Justice Department has traditionally sought criminal charges only in cases it expects to win. But such failures have become more common for the department under Trump, who has pushed prosecutors to seek indictments even in cases in which evidence is lacking.
While the Justice Department announced charges in recent days against two former FBI agents and former FBI Director James Comey, none of them were charged by a grand jury, a hurdle prosecutors will need to clear to move forward with a criminal prosecution.
Hutchinson, a former aide to Mark Meadows, a White House chief of staff during Trump’s first term, emerged as a key witness against Trump during the public hearings held by the special House committee that investigated Jan. 6.

Grand jury declines to bring charges against Cassidy Hutchinson
A federal grand jury in Washington today rejected an effort by the Justice Department to indict Cassidy Hutchinson, the former White House aide President Donald Trump targeted after she gave damning testimony to a congressional committee investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, according to people briefed on the matter.
The rejection of the indictment — known in legal circles as a “no true bill” — was the latest extraordinary setback in Trump’s wide-ranging campaign to go after his political opponents. The Justice Department has repeatedly failed to build criminal indictments against the president’s rivals.
Some Justice Department prosecutors had been deeply skeptical that there was a case to be made against Hutchinson, concluding that it would be difficult to win a conviction against her.
But in an unusual arrangement, the investigation was directed to the department’s civil rights division, which normally focuses on issues like police violence and election integrity. The civil rights division is led by Harmeet Dhillon, a Trump loyalist who has effectively reoriented the unit to align with Trump’s agenda, including by extracting agreements from elite universities that were favorable to the administration.
It was once rare for grand jurors to rebuff prosecutors and turn down a request for an indictment, given that the Justice Department has traditionally sought criminal charges only in cases it expects to win. But such failures have become more common for the department under Trump, who has pushed prosecutors to seek indictments even in cases in which evidence is lacking.
While the Justice Department announced charges in recent days against two former FBI agents and former FBI Director James Comey, none of them were charged by a grand jury, a hurdle prosecutors will need to clear to move forward with a criminal prosecution.

Hutchinson, a former aide to Mark Meadows, a White House chief of staff during Trump’s first term, emerged as a key witness against Trump during the public hearings held by the special House committee that investigated Jan. 6.
She had been seen as a Trump loyalist. But during her testimony, which was watched by more than 13 million Americans, she portrayed Trump as a leader willing to do almost anything to cling to power.
Among Hutchinson’s disclosures was how Trump, despite knowing that the crowd assembled on the National Mall might have been armed and violent, encouraged people to march toward the Capitol.
Hutchinson also testified about a conversation she heard in the White House that recounted Trump lunging at a Secret Service agent inside his protective vehicle, after he was told that he could not join his supporters at the Capitol for security reasons.
Hutchinson made clear during her testimony that her account about Trump’s behavior in the vehicle came to her secondhand. It was later contradicted by some of the Secret Service agents assigned to protect the president. When the special counsel, Jack Smith, indicted Trump in 2023 on charges of seeking to overturn the results of the 2020 election, he did not rely on Hutchinson as a witness.
The attempt to indict Hutchinson was the administration’s latest bid to use the vast prosecutorial powers of the federal government against Trump’s perceived enemies. Many of those efforts have failed as judges and grand juries have pushed back.
Charges brought by the Justice Department last year against Comey and Letitia James, the New York attorney general, were thrown out by a judge who ruled that the prosecutor handpicked by Trump to file the indictments had been improperly appointed.
Still, the Justice Department pushed through a new indictment of Comey in April, accusing him of threatening the president by posting a photograph of seashells on a beach in North Carolina spelling a message: “86 47.” Prosecutors say that “86” was a mafia slang term for assassination, and that “47” referred to Trump’s position as the 47th president.
Other cases that Trump wanted built against former President Joe Biden and Jerome Powell, then the Federal Reserve chair, fell apart in the investigative stage, before they could be presented to grand juries.
And in February, a federal grand jury in Washington rejected an indictment against six Democratic lawmakers Trump wanted targeted. Those lawmakers, who had worked in the military and intelligence communities, put out videos in which they reminded intelligence and miliary personnel that they were obligated to refuse illegal orders.

The Justice Department just hit a major wall in its effort to indict Cassidy Hutchinson.
A federal grand jury in Washington reportedly refused to return an indictment against the former White House aide, whose testimony became one of the most explosive moments of the House January 6 committee’s televised hearings.
The rejection is especially striking because grand juries hear the prosecution’s evidence without a defense team in the room, and the government only needs to establish probable cause rather than prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
But even that lower threshold was reportedly not met.
Breaking: A grand jury rejected the DOJ’s attempt to indict former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson, according to people familiar with the matter…
— The Washington Post (@washingtonpost) October 27, 2026
The Washington Post reported Tuesday that the grand jury declined the Justice Department’s attempt to charge Hutchinson over the account she gave lawmakers concerning President Trump’s actions on January 6, 2021. The report attributed the development to people familiar with the matter because grand-jury proceedings are secret.
That means there is no public indictment laying out an exact criminal theory, no trial date and no court finding that Hutchinson committed a crime. Prosecutors could still try to present the matter again, but the reported refusal is an unmistakable setback for a case the department had been building for months.
The investigation came into public view earlier this year after House Republicans referred Hutchinson to the Justice Department over allegations that she had lied to Congress.
By early October, prosecutors were no longer merely reviewing documents behind closed doors. The Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division had begun presenting evidence to a federal grand jury in Washington.
Another Trump prosecution crumbles as the grand jury declines to indict Cassidy Hutchinson…
— Tom Hamburger (@thamburger) October 27, 2026
CBS News independently reported on October 8 that federal prosecutors were presenting evidence to a Washington grand jury examining whether Hutchinson may have lied in her testimony. Two sources familiar with the matter confirmed the grand-jury activity, while the precise charges under consideration remained unclear.
The network also noted that Hutchinson had served as an aide to White House Chief of Staff Mark Meadows before becoming the committee witness whose account drew national attention in June 2022.
The most famous part of Hutchinson’s testimony concerned what she said she had been told about President Trump’s presidential vehicle after his speech at the Ellipse.
Hutchinson did not claim to have witnessed the alleged incident herself. She testified that White House Deputy Chief of Staff Anthony Ornato told her Trump became angry when the Secret Service would not take him to the Capitol, reached toward the steering wheel and moved toward the head of his security detail.
That account quickly became one of the committee’s biggest headlines.
It also became one of its most heavily disputed claims.
The Secret Service driver later told investigators that he did not see Trump grab the steering wheel or lunge toward the front seat. Other witnesses described the president as angry about being taken back to the White House, but did not corroborate the physical confrontation Hutchinson recounted.
House Republicans later widened their scrutiny beyond the vehicle story.
Breaking News: A federal grand jury declined to indict Cassidy Hutchinson over her January 6 testimony…
— The New York Times (@nytimes) October 27, 2026
The House Committee on Administration said an independent handwriting analyst concluded that a proposed January 6 message Hutchinson testified she had written was instead penned by White House lawyer Eric Herschmann. The committee argued that the analysis contradicted Hutchinson’s sworn testimony and her later account of the note in her book.

Hutchinson and her defenders have maintained that she truthfully relayed what she remembered and what others told her, while critics argued that the January 6 committee rushed sensational claims into a public hearing without adequate corroboration.
Those disputes gave federal prosecutors a politically explosive but legally difficult case.
To bring a criminal charge based on false testimony, the government would have needed to identify a specific statement, show that it was material and establish probable cause that Hutchinson knowingly lied. A conflict between witnesses, or proof that an underlying secondhand story was inaccurate, would not automatically establish that Hutchinson deliberately gave false testimony about what she had been told.
That distinction may help explain why the Justice Department came up empty before the grand jury.
For now, Hutchinson has not been indicted, and the department has no public criminal case against her.

The Justice Department spent months examining one of the most controversial witnesses from the January 6 hearings.
When the case finally reached the people empowered to authorize charges, they reportedly said no.

The Justice Department on Tuesday failed to secure a grand jury indictment against a former White House staffer who provided dramatic but disputed testimony against President Donald Trump before a House committee investigating the January 6, 2021, U.S. Capitol insurrection, according to two people familiar with the matter.
A grand jury in Washington rejected prosecutors’ request to return an indictment against Cassidy Hutchinson, said the people, who spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the case. It’s the latest setback in the Justice Department's efforts to persuade grand jurors in the nation's capital to bring politically sensitive cases.
Details of prosecutors’ allegations against Hutchinson were not immediately clear, but Republican lawmakers had accused her of lying under oath in her explosive testimony in 2022 about Trump’s behavior on Jan. 6, when a mob of his supporters stormed the Capitol to halt the congressional certification of his election loss to Democrat Joe Biden.
The effort to indict Hutchinson was hardly isolated. It is part of a surge in politically sensitive actions by the Justice Department in the run-up to next week’s midterm elections targeting perceived adversaries of the president, including a new attempt to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey and a search by federal agents of the home of outspoken Trump critic and Democratic U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota.

It's highly unusual for grand juries to decline to return indictments, but the Justice Department under Trump has been rebuked by citizens in the nation's capital in a number of high-profile cases. A grand jury in Washington earlier this year declined to indict Democratic lawmakers in connection with a video they recorded urging U.S. service members to follow established military protocols and reject orders they believe to be unlawful.
An attorney for Hutchinson didn't immediately return a phone message seeking comment Tuesday.
Hutchinson said Trump was angry and defiant on Jan. 6
Hutchinson's testimony, at a surprise hearing announced just 24 hours earlier, was seen at the time as particularly powerful given her proximity to power as special assistant to Mark Meadows, Trump’s chief of staff.
Hutchinson described an angry, defiant president who was trying to let armed protesters avoid security screenings at a rally that morning to protest his 2020 election defeat and who later grabbed at the steering wheel of the presidential SUV when the Secret Service refused to let him go to the Capitol. And when the events at the Capitol spiraled toward violence, with the crowd chanting “Hang Mike Pence,” she testified that Trump declined to intervene.
Trump at the time denied much of what Hutchinson said on his social media platform, Truth Social. He called her a “total phony” and “bad news.”

Federal prosecutors investigating former Trump White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson have reportedly encountered a setback in their effort to bring criminal charges over her testimony to the House committee investigating the January 6, 2021, Capitol riot.

The investigation was being handled by the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division rather than the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, an unusual assignment for a case involving potential false statements to Congress.
Hutchinson previously worked as an aide to former White House chief of staff Mark Meadows during Trump’s first administration.
She attracted national attention June 28, 2022, when she testified before the House select committee investigating the Capitol riot.
During that hearing, Hutchinson told lawmakers that Trump had been informed some supporters attending his January 6 rally were carrying weapons but nevertheless wanted them admitted to the event.

According to Hutchinson’s testimony, Ornato told her that Trump attempted to grab the steering wheel of the presidential vehicle and lunged toward a Secret Service agent.
Hutchinson did not claim to have personally witnessed the alleged confrontation inside the vehicle.
Her account subsequently came under scrutiny after the Secret Service driver disputed the description of a physical altercation.
The driver testified that Trump was upset about not being taken to the Capitol but said he did not see the president grab the steering wheel or lunge toward the front of the vehicle.
Republican lawmakers have cited those discrepancies in challenging Hutchinson’s credibility and the January 6 committee’s handling of her testimony.
Reps. Jim Jordan of Ohio and Barry Loudermilk of Georgia referred allegations concerning Hutchinson’s statements to the Justice Department for investigation.
The lawmakers argued that her testimony contained inconsistencies warranting criminal scrutiny.
However, conflicting witness accounts do not automatically establish that a person committed perjury. Prosecutors must establish that a statement was knowingly false and met the other elements of the applicable criminal statute.
An Oct. 9 report by WIRED stated that Justice Department officials had been considering perjury and obstruction-of-justice charges.

Prosecutors were also reportedly examining her account of a statement prepared for Trump during the Capitol riot, which former White House attorney Eric Herschmann has disputed.
According to WIRED, some Justice Department officials questioned whether the available evidence would satisfy the legal requirements for a successful prosecution.
The publication also reported that prosecutors might wait until after the November 3 midterm elections before seeking an indictment.
That reporting makes independent confirmation of the newly alleged grand jury rejection particularly important.
A federal grand jury is responsible for determining whether prosecutors have presented sufficient evidence to establish probable cause for criminal charges.
Under federal procedures, at least 12 grand jurors must agree before an indictment can be issued.
If grand jurors decline to indict, prosecutors generally may continue investigating or present additional evidence, subject to applicable legal restrictions.
A refusal to indict does not constitute an acquittal because no criminal trial has occurred.
Grand jury proceedings are ordinarily confidential, and information about unsuccessful indictment requests frequently becomes public through individuals familiar with the investigation rather than official court filings.
Hutchinson has not been publicly charged in connection with the investigation, and the Justice Department has not announced a completed prosecution against her.
The reported development comes amid continuing scrutiny of the administration’s efforts to pursue criminal investigations involving former federal officials and witnesses whose statements have drawn criticism from Trump and congressional Republicans.
Hutchinson has previously defended her congressional testimony and has maintained that she provided investigators with information to the best of her knowledge.
For now, the existence of the federal investigation and the grand jury’s earlier examination of evidence are supported by multiple news reports. The more recent assertion that grand jurors formally rejected an indictment remains unverified, leaving the current status of the charging decision uncertain.

Four sources briefed on the proceedings told CBS it was Hutchinson. The Washington Post first reported the decision.
A senior U.S. official confirmed the no bill to NBC News. Two people familiar with the matter told the Associated Press the same. According to NBC, the grand jury heard evidence in early October.
None of the outlets could say which charges prosecutors sought. CBS could not determine which parts of her testimony drew scrutiny. Hutchinson has maintained that she testified truthfully, NBC reported.
The courtroom disclosure followed a new rule. In March, Chief Judge James Boasberg ordered that the duty magistrate judge hear about every grand jury refusal in Washington, Fox News reported. That applies even when the person already faces charges, and the notices stay under seal.
Eleven no bills in a year of 193,000 suspects
A federal grand jury has 16 to 23 members. It “may indict only if at least 12 jurors concur,” under Rule 6 of the federal criminal rules.
Its question is narrow. The Justice Manual describes the job as deciding whether there is probable cause. The jurors have two choices: indict, or return a no bill.
That low bar explains why refusals almost never happen. The clearest federal count we found comes from the Bureau of Justice Statistics. Its report Federal Justice Statistics, 2010 tracks how U.S. attorneys closed out their matters in fiscal 2010.
That year, U.S. attorneys concluded matters involving 193,021 suspects. They took 48.4% of them to federal district court and declined 30,670.
Table 2.3 lists the reasons for those declinations. “No true bill returned” appears exactly 11 times. Against the roughly 93,000 suspects prosecuted in district court, that works out to about one in 8,500.
Two caveats apply. The figure is 16 years old. It also counts only matters that prosecutors dropped after a no bill, not cases they took to a second grand jury. Still, it is the only official breakdown we located, and it shows how far outside the norm Tuesday’s vote sits.
Prosecutors can try again, with a sign-off
A no bill is not an acquittal. NBC reported that the decision does not bar the Justice Department from seeking charges against Hutchinson again.
The department’s own rules add one hurdle. Section 9-11.120 of the manual covers what happens after a no bill. Prosecutors “should not” take it to another grand jury, or back to the same one, “without first securing the approval of the responsible United States Attorney.”
The same chapter sets a second duty. Prosecutors who know of “substantial evidence that directly negates the guilt” of a subject must present it before seeking an indictment. Nobody outside the grand jury room knows whether that happened here.
Time also matters. Most federal crimes carry a five-year limit under Section 3282 of the criminal code. Hutchinson testified in public on June 28, 2022.
For anything she said that day, the window would close in late June 2027. Without knowing the charges, treat that date as an estimate.
The department has gone back before. After a judge dismissed the first case against New York Attorney General Letitia James on technical grounds, prosecutors tried three more times to indict her, NBC reported. Grand juries refused each time.
There is a second route, too. In the third case against James Comey, prosecutors filed a criminal information. A prosecutor writes and signs that charge, and no grand jury votes on it. For a felony, it only works if the defendant waives indictment, and Comey has not.
The secondhand steering-wheel story at the center
Hutchinson worked as a special assistant to Trump’s chief of staff, Mark Meadows. The committee announced her hearing about 24 hours in advance, according to the AP. She described Trump on Jan. 6, 2021, as angry and defiant.
NBC reported that she quoted Trump as saying, “I don’t f—ing care that they have weapons.” He wanted the metal detectors at his rally removed, she testified. She also said Trump wanted to go to the Capitol.
The most disputed part was something she did not see. CBS reported that she relayed an account from then-deputy chief of staff Tony Ornato. In it, Trump lunged at the steering wheel after his lead Secret Service agent refused to drive him to the Capitol. She acknowledged at the time that she had no firsthand knowledge of the episode, according to the AP.
In March 2024, House Republicans released the committee’s interview with the Secret Service officer who drove the SUV. The public had not seen it before. He said he did not see the altercation and that Trump “never grabbed the steering wheel,” the AP reported.
The AP added that the transcript also backed up other parts of her account, including Trump’s push to go to the Capitol. So the sharpest dispute centers on a story she told the committee came secondhand. House Republican allies of the president referred the matter to the Justice Department, according to media reports cited by CBS.
Trump has called Hutchinson a “scam artist” who lied under oath, NBC reported. In 2022, he wrote on Truth Social: “What is the Justice Department going to do about this?”
A Civil Rights Division case, and a pattern in Washington
The Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division ran the case, according to NBC. Trump appointee Harmeet Dhillon heads the division. It traditionally enforces civil rights and antidiscrimination laws, which makes it an unusual home for a false-testimony inquiry.
The AP called the no bill “the latest setback” in the department’s efforts to charge people Trump sees as adversaries. NBC listed others. A grand jury also refused to indict six Democratic members of Congress over a video telling military and intelligence personnel not to obey unlawful orders. According to Fox News, that case prompted Boasberg’s March order.
Attorney General Todd Blanche defended the record in April. He told NBC the failed prosecutions showed “that we’re working hard.” He added: “It could be that the grand jury just made the wrong decision.”
The vote comes a week before the November 3 midterms. Other Justice Department inquiries, such as the reported investigation of Corey Lewandowski, remain in the news.
For now, Hutchinson faces no charge. Under the Justice Manual, any second attempt needs a U.S. attorney’s approval before it goes back to a grand jury.
